items.title: The ELIZA effect
items.claim: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA chatbot (1966) used simple keyword matching. What was Weizenbaum's reaction when his secretary engaged emotionally with it?

options.text: He was thrilled and commercialised it
He became a sharp critic of attributing understanding to machines

items.reveal_title: ELIZA's creator turned into one of AI's earliest critics
items.reveal:
Weizenbaum's 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason argued against using computers in roles requiring human judgement.

The 'ELIZA effect' describes the human tendency to attribute understanding to systems that have none.
items.why: Creators often see clearly what users want to project. The pattern recurs with each new generation of chatbots.

items.title: 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE 754
items.claim: In most programming languages using IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic, what does 0.1 + 0.2 evaluate to?
items.reveal:
Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary representation. The standard IEEE 754 double evaluates the sum to 0.30000000000000004.

Decimal or arbitrary-precision libraries are used where this matters (finance, audit).
items.why: Numerical errors emerge from representation, not arithmetic mistakes.

items.title: The first computer 'bug'
items.claim: In 1947 a literal insect was taped into a log book at Harvard. Who was the engineer most associated with the incident?
items.reveal_title: Grace Hopper's team at Harvard Mark II
items.reveal:
A moth was found jamming a relay in the Mark II computer on 9 September 1947 and taped into the log with the note 'First actual case of bug being found'.

The term 'bug' had been used in engineering since at least Edison.
items.why: Terminology often predates its famous origin story; jargon collects illustrative anecdotes.
